messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai had always been a man who found solace in his art. As a painter, he spent most of his days lost in the vibrant colors and textures of his canvases. But that all changed on a fateful day seven years ago when Kai was caught in a terrorist attack while visiting family in his native Fiji. The sounds of gunfire and screams still echoed in his mind, transporting him back to the moment when he had to shield himself behind a nearby wall as the world around him descended into chaos. In the aftermath of that event, Kai began to notice that memories of that day would force their way into his mind at the most inopportune moments. He'd be standing at his easel, brush poised over canvas, when suddenly he'd feel his body tense up and he'd be back in that alleyway, huddled behind a wall as bullets whizzed by. These bodily reenactments were so vivid that Kai would often find himself instinctively ducking for cover or crouching low to the ground, much to the confusion of those around him. As these memories continued to intrude on his daily life, Kai started to develop some very negative appraisals about himself and the world. He began to feel like he couldn't rely on himself to stay safe, that at any moment something terrible could happen again. And as for others? Forget it – they were just as powerless as he was in the face of such senseless violence. The world, Kai had come to believe, was a fundamentally dangerous place. These negative appraisals only seemed to fuel his memories, making them even more vivid and unsettling. In an effort to cope with these feelings, Kai started seeking reassurance from those around him. He'd constantly ask his friends and family if they thought he was okay, if they thought the world was a safe place. And when that didn't work, he tried to exert strict control over his emotions, as if by sheer willpower alone he could keep the memories at bay. But of course, this only made things worse. The more Kai sought reassurance, the more he seemed to doubt himself. He became convinced that others were just humoring him, that they secretly thought he was weak or foolish for still being so traumatized after all these years. And as for controlling his emotions? That was a losing battle from the start. The memories would always find a way to break through, leaving Kai feeling like he was at their mercy. As time went on, Kai found himself avoiding going out more and more. He'd stop attending art openings or visiting with friends, afraid of what might happen if he left the safety of his own home. His painting suffered as well – how could he possibly create anything beautiful when the world outside seemed so full of darkness? It was this downward spiral that finally led Kai to seek help. He realized that he couldn't keep living like this, constantly on edge and waiting for the other shoe to drop. What scared him most was losing himself entirely to these memories and negative appraisals – becoming a shadow of his former self. And yet, as he sat in the therapist's office, clutching his worn-out paint-stained apron, Kai couldn't help but feel a glimmer of hope that maybe, just maybe, there was still a way out of this darkness.
